summary: TAP identifies agents on card-not-present purchases and moves no money, so the rules that bite are card-payment rules: who authorized the transaction (Regulation E and Z, PSD2, UK PSRs), strong customer authentication when the user is absent, and data protection for the IP address, device data and contact values that the consumer object sends to merchants. Visa's rules, which govern Visa and its member institutions and yield to applicable law, have since 2025-10-18 made the cardholder responsible, within Visa's system, for an Agentic Payment Provider's actions. Visa calls none of its rules a liability shift, though issuers must pay for Agentic Transactions made under the cardholder's instructions; Worldpay (2026-07-30) says no liability shift exists yet. The Product Terms put consumer disclosures and consents on the implementer. Rows are dated; check each source before relying on it.

rows.text: Card-not-present purchases by a recognized agent fall under Regulation Z for credit cards: unauthorized use means use without actual, implied or apparent authority, with cardholder liability capped at the lesser of $50 or the amount before notice. Whether an agent acting outside its instruction has apparent authority is untested.

For debit cards, Regulation E excludes transfers by a person the consumer gave the access device to, until the consumer revokes that authority, so a consumer may carry an agent's transfers until notice. TAP itself carries no consent record.
TAP adds no sanctions or AML layer; card payments it accompanies follow the issuer's and acquirer's existing programs. OFAC obligations are the same whatever the channel.
California's CCPA regulations on automated decisionmaking technology take effect from 2026-01-01; a merchant that uses contextualData or the ID Token in automated decisions should check them.

The RTS on strong customer authentication requires two factors and dynamic linking for remote payments. Visa says every Agentic Ready transaction in Europe used Visa Payment Passkeys to support SCA; that authentication sits in VIC, not in TAP.

PSD2 makes a payment authorized only with the payer's consent and caps payer liability for unauthorized transactions. How consent to a specific transaction applies to an agent instruction is untested; PSD3 and the PSR (provisional agreement 2025-11-27) add no agent rules and are not yet in the Official Journal.

contextualData sends the consumer's IP address, device data, country and postal code to each merchant, and the ID Token carries a stable subject id and obfuscated contact values; under the GDPR these are generally personal data. The TAP Product Terms put disclosures and consents on the implementer.

The AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2026-08-02; the Digital Omnibus moved Annex III high-risk duties to 2027-12-02. A shopping agent is not high-risk by default, but its operator may need to tell people they deal with an AI system.
The Payment Services Regulations 2017 treat a payment as authorized only with the payer's consent (regulation 67) and cap payer liability at GBP 35 in many cases (regulation 77).
HM Treasury's consultation on modernising payment services regulation (2026-07-14 to 2026-10-06) asks how authentication, consent and liability should adapt for agentic payments; no response yet.
The FCA said on 2026-03-25 it will consider with HM Treasury whether regulation must change to support agentic AI payments; there is no AI statute.
PIPEDA governs the personal information in the consumer object that Canadian merchants receive.
No agent-specific payment liability rule was found in Canada; consumer-driven banking phase 2 is targeted for mid-2027.
MAS's E-Payments User Protection Guidelines allocate liability for unauthorized and erroneous e-payments; they do not address agents specifically.

MAS issued Guidelines on AI Risk Management on 2026-10-07, effective 2027-10-07, naming agentic AI systems; Ant International, Mastercard and Visa announced Know Your Agent work through a MAS-convened platform on 2026-09-11, building on TAP (reported).

Visa's rules govern Visa and its member institutions and yield to applicable law. Since 2025-10-18 they have required an Agentic Payment Provider to enroll in Visa Intelligent Commerce and register with Visa, directly or via an Agentic Payment Enabler. Within Visa's system, the cardholder is responsible for the provider's actions in an Agentic Transaction as if the cardholder had initiated it, and the provider counts as the Cardholder for that transaction. A merchant must not require a cardholder to waive the right to dispute an Agentic Transaction. The rules do not mention TAP.

Visa calls no rule a liability shift and adds no agent-specific dispute condition, fee or interchange rate. It does require issuers to pay for Agentic Transactions made under a cardholder's payment instructions and not to block them wholesale. From 2026-10-24 it also accepts an Agentic Payment Provider's login ID among the evidence that can defeat a card-absent fraud dispute. Worldpay wrote on 2026-07-30 that no liability shift exists yet and that properly tokenized agent transactions follow existing rules.
EMVCo published a draft EMV Agentic Payments framework on 2026-09-01 and lists Know Your Agent and agentic transaction indicators as possible future work; TAP is not an EMVCo document.

A merchant that decrypts the payment payload receives a payment token, expiry and cardholder name, and key-entered checkout handles card numbers; the TAP specification says nothing about PCI DSS scope, while Visa offers Intelligent Commerce Connect to handle PCI compliance for enablers.
